transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-28
Time: 16:00 PDT
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Dana Morris (Redwood SE), Nina Lopez (Atlas Head of ML), Marcus Chen (Atlas Infra), Priya Rao (Atlas Security)

Auto-summary: quick walkthrough of Redwood Optimize UI and cost model. Focus on batching and KV/prefix caching recommendations, plus pilot next steps.

00:00 Samir: hey everyone, thanks for joining, can I get quick intros?
00:08 Nina: yeah nina lopez, head of ml at atlas, thanks for having us, we've been looking at optimizations for our LLM endpoints.
00:13 Samir: great, i'll hand to dana to kick off the optimize walkthrough, we'll show the UI and then dive into batching and kv cache cost model.
00:20 Dana: cool, so first quick context, three levers we usually recommend: batching, prefix caching and kv cache. here on the console you'll see the optimize tab, we profile your token distribution, and then give a recommended config, we also simulate cost impact.
00:40 Dana: a quick note, some transcripts spell KV as K V cash in earlier runs, so apologies if anything in the export looks funny, that is a common tts bug.
00:48 Marcus: ha, yes we've seen that in automated logs. main questions up front: latency SLO is 150ms P95 for most routes, and we care about cost per 1M tokens.
00:58 Samir: perfect, that's helpful, we'll keep latency constraints top of mind.
01:05 Dana: jumping into the cost model slide — assumption A: baseline no-batching, no-cache. assumption B: batching with 20ms wait, global max batch size 64. assumption C: kv cache with 45% effective hit-rate for our prefix-heavy prompts, ttl 24h, plus prefix cache for top-10 prompts.
01:30 Nina: 45% sounds optimistic — what's that based on?
01:33 Dana: good call, that's from similar financial Q&A workloads we've seen — longer repeated prefixes, identical transaction descriptions, etc. in the cost model we show low/med/high hit-rate bands: 25/45/65%. you can plug your observed prefix reuse in the console profiler.
01:52 Marcus: when you say prefix cache, is that cached tokens or cached activations? want to be concrete.
:56 Dana: prefix cache is replaying cached KV states — it's a warm KV cache that restores the decoder key/value cache, so subsequent generation only computes the suffix. it's cheaper than full recompute but has memory and serialization cost. the console shows memory per cached convo estimate.
02:20 Nina: and KV cache TTL of 24h — how do you handle updates, e.g., if the user data changes?
02:26 Dana: good question. you can either evict by key, or use versioned keys tied to the user profile. most customers choose short TTL for frequently updated data and longer TTL for static prompts.
02:38 Samir: also note our smart routing can route to a dedicated pool where cache pre-warming is easier because the model instance persists.
02:46 Marcus: that relates to infra cost — if we do dedicated vs hosted, what's the unit economics?
02:50 Dana: in the spreadsheet we'll send, we show per-hour GPU cost, expected tokens per second, and a net cost per 1M tokens with and without cache. quick example: on A100-equivalent dedicated pool the baseline cost is $X per 1M tokens, batching at wait=20ms reduces cost by ~18% on conversational loads, adding 45% kv hit-rate yields another ~30% savings vs baseline. those numbers are illustrative; they'll be populated with your telemetry in the pilot.
03:25 Nina: can you show the console simulation with our traffic profile?
03:28 Dana: sure, here in the profiler you can upload a sample trace or paste a token length distribution. i'll toggle to Atlas profile — note: the profiler is sampling, so it will estimate hit-rate and batching benefit.
03:45 Dana: see here, average seq length 220 tokens, 60% of calls have a repeated prefix (>30 tokens). predicted batching window of 15-25ms hits 65% of request arrival patterns for batch sizes up to 32.
04:05 Marcus: so the tradeoff is chaining a small wait time to collect the batch which can add tail latency, correct?
04:08 Dana: yes, exactly. you can set two knobs: max_wait_ms and max_batch_size. for strict SLOs we suggest dynamic batching with JSY greedy thresholding — default 20ms and fallback to single-request mode at P99 limits.
04:25 Nina: what about streaming vs non-streaming responses — does batching break streaming?
04:29 Dana: streaming can be preserved; we stream partial tokens for a batch but network-level ordering means some requests might see earlier chunks later. for strict real-time feel we sometimes recommend lower batch windows and larger KV cache to compensate.
04:43 Samir: quick aside on quantization: moving from FP16 to 4-bit quant gives headroom to run more concurrent requests on the same GPU which amplifies batching savings; Optimize will propose quantization profiles per model.
04:59 Marcus: are there any memory limits to how many KV entries we can hold if we use aggressive caching?
05:03 Dana: yes we show estimated RAM/VRAM per cached convo. on a 80GB GPU, typical Atlas config with top-5k active users may require ~20GB of KV storage for a 24h TTL. we can also offload cold entries to a managed redis-backed store with a small restore penalty.
05:25 Priya: from security, how are those cached keys encrypted at rest and how do we audit access?
05:30 Samir: we support customer-managed KMS and HSM integration for key encryption, and all cache operations emit audit logs that you can forward to your SIEM. we'll share the SOC2 and KMS docs.
05:42 Priya: good, please share retention and log schemas.
05:45 Samir: will do.
06:00 Dana: back to the cost model: i'll show the spreadsheet we use. baseline tokens, model throughput, GPU cost/hr, batch efficiency factor, kv hit-rate, serialize/deserialize penalty, net token compute saved. i'll also show a sensitivity table.
06:20 Dana: example table: baseline 1M tokens costs $120 (toy number), batching reduces compute ops by 18% => $98, kv 45% hit-rate reduces compute by another 30% => $68 net. that doesn't include storage or network egress which are small but listed.
06:40 Nina: can you break out where the 30% comes from? is that 30% of compute time or token-level reduction?
06:44 Dana: it's token-level compute reduction: if 45% of tokens are served from cache, you save the forward-pass compute for those tokens. there is a serialization cost around 2-5ms per restore, so net latency effect depends on concurrency.
07:02 Marcus: what about cold-start for the cache after a deploy — is there a warmup strategy?
07:06 Dana: yes we recommend a pre-warm job that replays recent conversations into the cache during deploy, or we can run background prefetch on first N users. it's built into the Dedicated deployment workflow.
07:20 Nina: ok walking through the UI, i see the recommended config — it suggests prefix cache for top-10 templates, kv cache ttl 24h, batching wait 20ms, max batch 64, quantize to 4-bit. can you explain the template selection?
07:35 Dana: the profiler ranks repeated prompt patterns and recommends top templates by traffic volume and token-length. prefix cache is best for long identical prefixes; kv cache helps when the prefix is long but suffix differs.
07:48 Nina: does the optimizer propose per-route overrides? we have some admin routes that need strict latency.
07:53 Dana: yes you can set route-level policies; Optimize recommends global defaults and per-route overrides. for admin routes we often recommend bypass batching (or very low wait) and rely more on dedicated instances.
08:05 Marcus: what metrics do you advise we monitor in the pilot?
08:09 Samir: key metrics: P50/P95 latency, token throughput, batch fill rate, KV hit-rate, bytes per second for cache traffic, and cost per 1M tokens. we'll provide dashboards and trace hooks.
08:22 Nina: can we run a small pilot with a 2-week window to see real numbers?
08:25 Dana: yes, we usually do 1-2 week pilots. for Atlas we'd run a dedicated pool with the pilot dataset and run a compare vs baseline window.
08:35 Samir: i'll send a proposed pilot scope and hardware sizing.
08:38 Marcus: network and firewall wise we will need a peering/ip allowlist and a small NAT egress plan.
08:43 Samir: understood, Dana will coordinate with Marcus on connectivity details.
08:50 Priya: just to confirm, audit logs will include cache restore events?
08:54 Dana: yes, every restore and eviction is logged with key id and timestamp, and we can include user id if you enable tracing.
09:05 Nina: show me an example run: what does end-to-end look like for a typical query?
09:08 Dana: so user hits API -> load balancer -> request routed to model instance. Optimize's runtime checks prefix cache key; on miss it goes to model compute, generates tokens. if there is a batch, multiple requests are combined into one forward pass with position offsets handled by the runtime. when restore occurs it loads the cached KV into GPU memory then runs only suffix. logs then emit token breakdown.
09:34 Marcus: in the output logs how granular are token counts? do we get per-request token-level billing?
09:38 Dana: yes per-request token counts, and per-token breakdown in the cost analytics.
09:45 Nina: what about partially overlapping prefixes (similar but not identical) — can the cache do fuzzy matches?
09:49 Dana: not fuzzy at the KV layer — it's exact keying. for similar prompts we recommend a prefix normalization step or use of template extraction before caching. the console has a small toolkit to surface candidate normalizations.
10:05 Marcus: what about multi-tenant isolation in dedicated pools — can one tenant's cache affect another?
10:09 Dana: dedicated pools are single-tenant by design. we also support per-tenant vhosts in hosted mode with strict isolation.
10:16 Priya: any notes on PII in cache? can we redact?
10:19 Dana: yes we recommend token-level redaction prior to caching or using hashed keys with a mapping outside the model. we can also disable cache for routes that touch PII.
10:30 Nina: okay, can you walk through the sensitivity analysis in the spreadsheet?
10:33 Dana: yes, column A is hit-rate band (25/45/65), column B is batch window (10/20/50ms), column C is net compute saved. the tornado chart shows kv hit-rate has the largest single impact, batching next.
10:48 Samir: i'll drop an example row with Atlas numbers later but here's a quick back-of-envelope: if you push the batch wait to 50ms you might get higher batch fill but risk pushing P95 over 150ms; we usually recommend aggressive cache first, mild batching second.
11:05 Nina: so recommendation: start with kv cache for the top-10 templates, set batching wait to 20ms, run pilot, and only raise batching if latency is well below SLO.
11:12 Dana: exactly. that reduces your downside in case hit-rates are lower than expected.
11:18 Marcus: any operational downsides we should be aware of? e.g., cache corruption or restore failures?
11:22 Dana: restore failures are rare; we have retries and fallbacks to full compute. all operations are idempotent. the runtime will emit fallback metrics.
11:30 Nina: how long to stand up a dedicated pilot environment?
11:33 Dana: typically 3-5 business days once we have access and datasets, faster if you already have peering and credentials ready.
11:40 Samir: ok next steps recap — we'll send the cost model spreadsheet, SOC2/KMS docs, and a pilot proposal. Dana will coordinate the benchmark window and Marcus will share network requirements. Priya will confirm audit retention.
11:55 Priya: noted.
12:00 Nina: one last question — are there limits on number of cached keys per instance?
12:04 Dana: practical limits depend on VRAM but we recommend sharded cache with an LRU and a cap; console will give recommended caps based on your active user estimate.
12:20 Marcus: thanks, this was helpful.
12:24 Samir: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the spreadsheet and a calendar invite for the pilot planning session.
12:30 Meeting end.
